title: Can this coat go back?

beats.say: Bob hangs a returned coat over August twelfth. The receipt says July twenty-fifth. Trace the tape back to the purchase. How many days has the customer had this coat? Eighteen.

Bob had a fourteen-day rule open before the app restarted. The screen clears. He reopens the saved policy file. Put a finger on day fourteen. The coat hangs past it. Another saved edition gives thirty days. The coat is inside that window.

Which rule can Bob quote on August twelfth? To fill the return slip, we need a paragraph from Harbor, in force for the request, that Bob has permission to read. Then we can trace his answer back to its source.

title: Where did the paragraph survive?

beats.say: SQL lets us read and change rows in a relational database. A table groups rows with the same named fields, or columns. Here the chunks table has one row per paragraph. Read across this row. Its ID is c7a, its source document is d7, and its text sets the deadline. Commit saves the row in the database file.

Now start with an empty screen. Open a new connection to the same file and read the row back. The paragraph still points to the same document. That recovery depends on where the file lives. If a container can disappear, the file needs storage that survives the container.

You can check this in the article’s SQLite lab. Its sample file holds Acme’s API policies. Save the IDs from Bob’s search, commit, and close the connection. Reopen the same file and run the same search. The two IDs come back without loading any seed data.
Let’s follow the document link on the paragraph at Harbor.

title: Give each fact an identity and a relationship

beats.say: Store the source once, then let each paragraph carry its document identity. Follow the matching fields to the document, and from there to Harbor's workspace. A separate permission row says Bob may read this paragraph. These links are data the database can check.

A primary key gives a row its identity. Try inserting this identity a second time. The database rejects the duplicate. A new chunk must name its source. The document field is required, and SQLite checks its foreign key as soon as we insert the row.
Point the chunk at a missing document and that insertion fails too. In this lab we turn on SQLite’s foreign key checks on every new connection, before the transaction begins.

title: Which rows will SQLite accept?

beats.say: The SQLite lab uses Acme’s API policy. Follow one grant across its chunk, its document, and its workspace. The document holds the title, source key, and validity dates. Each chunk holds its own text. Bob can have a grant on one chunk and none on the next.
The chunk and the reader together identify a grant, so inserting that pair twice fails. CREATE TABLE sets up those rules. INSERT asks the database to check a new row against them.

Try these three inserts separately. The first chunk lacks an ID. The second names a document that never arrived. The third copies an existing paragraph into a different document. Check the ID, then the parent, then the document and text together. Only the copy gets through.

The same words can occur in different editions. This database requires a text primary key to be non-null explicitly. An ordinary SQLite rowid table otherwise allows a null text primary key. A required parent also needs a non-null reference.
Declaring that foreign key in a column lets SQLite check it. Putting a document ID in optional JSON metadata buys you no such check.
Now look at a score column with a check that the score is positive. Which of these values could you store?

Read the check results. Zero makes the expression false, so its insert fails. For a missing score the expression is unknown. SQLite lets that row through. Add a separate requirement that a score must be present. Only the missing score changes outcome.
In the policy tables, passing the structural checks tells us the links exist. We still need to check the source and Bob’s grant before he quotes it.

title: What goes in the question-mark slot?

beats.say: Bob wants the identities and titles of the policies on file at Harbor. SELECT names the fields to return. WHERE tells the database which documents to keep. Bind the store identity into the question-mark slot. Now test each document in order. All three Harbor versions come through, including the retired one. Birch stays out.

Try searching for children's coats. The apostrophe travels with the words in the bound value. SQL still sees the same statement, and none of our paragraphs contain that phrase. Now search for the percent sign on a discount notice.

In ten percent, mark the printed percent sign with an exclamation point. Put a wildcard on each end. Bind the escaped pattern to the one question mark. Now try the field name document underscore ID. Mark the underscore as literal. Bind the new pattern to that same slot.

title: Which passages contain the printed policy code?

beats.say: A customer copied this policy code from a notice. Look at the middle passage. Its X could fit an underscore wildcard. The letters after ten could fit a percent wildcard. Here the punctuation has to match the print, and the search ignores ASCII letter case.

The printed code is policy underscore ten percent exclamation point. Double the exclamation point first. It also serves as our escape mark. Mark the underscore and percent as literal. Put a wildcard at each end to allow words around the code. Which passages match?

Read down the three passages. The first has the code by itself. In the second, the X breaks the match. In the last passage, even the capital letters match. The outer wildcards let the extra words sit on either side.
Clear the search box. The helper trims the input and returns an empty list for a blank search. Otherwise the two outside wildcards could match every passage.

title: Build a citation from matching row fields

beats.say: The paragraph alone gives us text. A citation also needs its source title and version. A JOIN combines rows whose named fields satisfy a condition. Compare the paragraph's document reference with each document identity. Which source belongs beside this paragraph?

The matching identity selects the return-policy document. Move its title beside the text and we have a citable result. The receipt paragraph follows the same source. Matching a key identifies the exact version, even when an older document has the same title.

title: Keep unknown and not-yet-active separate

beats.say: NULL represents missing or unknown information. Comparing an end field to NULL with equals produces unknown rather than true, so WHERE does not keep that row. Use IS NULL for the open-end branch, joined with the earlier-than-end test by OR.
Then combine that whole branch with start less than or equal to the request time. A future version with an empty end still fails its start condition.

Our SQLite program stores fixed-width UTC timestamps with the same precision and Z suffix. Their text order matches chronological order under that convention. Arbitrary offsets and mixed formats need normalization rather than raw string comparison. The PostgreSQL extension sketch uses timestamp with time zone to compare instants.

Ten in the morning UTC and noon at plus two hours identify the same instant. PostgreSQL compares those instants. If the original time-zone name matters, save it separately. A move to a shared server also changes the driver’s placeholders and the transaction contract.

title: Put the request inside the version's interval

beats.say: Our fictional store changed its return window in July. Both editions contain the word return. Place the request time on their intervals. The earlier edition ends exactly where the next begins. At that boundary, which edition should supply the answer?

Include the start and exclude the end. The newer edition owns the boundary and this August request. Its empty end field means the end is unknown, so SQL uses IS NULL. Also check that the version has already started. Uniqueness of a start time alone allows overlapping intervals.

title: Can two editions cover the same day?

beats.say: These two Harbor editions meet on July first. For each store and policy, the database requires a different start date for each edition. Try adding an edition that runs from June fifteenth to July fifteenth. Its start date is new, and its end comes after its start.
Both checks pass. Look at June twentieth. Two editions cover that day. Move to July tenth. The proposal overlaps the July edition there. A unique start date still leaves Bob with two answers.

Watch how Harbor replaces an edition in August. The publisher runs BEGIN IMMEDIATE to take SQLite’s writer slot before it checks the open edition. It closes that edition exactly where the replacement starts. It saves the new document, paragraphs and grants in the same transaction.
At commit, the two intervals meet on August twelfth. Every publisher needs to follow that sequence. A second writer can wait for the slot or retry.

title: Which paragraphs reach Bob’s desk?

beats.say: For this test, the request names Bob and Harbor. All five paragraphs match the word return. Even the seven-day paragraph has a grant for Bob. For his Harbor request on August twelfth, before the new edition is published, which paragraphs belong on the slip?

Check Bob's grant first. Only Alice has the staff grant. Next require Harbor's workspace. That takes Birch’s seven-day rule out of this request even though Bob can read it there. Finally check the active version. Harbor once allowed thirty days, but that edition ended in July.

Move the two admitted paragraphs into the answer context. Bob has a deadline and a receipt instruction, both from the July edition. In production the server must identify Bob through his session and verify that he may serve Harbor. The same checks belong on a search by meaning.

title: Test the database role that runs the query

beats.say: Application predicates are one boundary; PostgreSQL row-level security can add another. When row security is enabled and no applicable policy permits rows, an ordinary subject role has a default-deny result. A policy must derive the principal and workspace from trusted request context.
Client-supplied reader names or workspace fields cannot grant themselves access merely by entering a query parameter.

Test the role the server actually uses. Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles bypass row security. Table owners normally bypass it too; FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY can subject the owner to the policies, while superuser and BYPASSRLS exceptions remain.

A successful test under an unrestricted owner is not a test of the application’s restricted role. Keep the same forbidden row in the fixture and exercise every retrieval route before adding it to answer context.

title: Group the rows before counting them

beats.say: We can ask a different question of the same rows: how many current paragraphs does each source contain? Filter by workspace and time, then collect matching document identities into groups. COUNT reduces each group to one result.
Harbor has two return-policy paragraphs, and its staff guide contributes one. An ingestion audit has to account for drafts too.

Here’s a draft with no paragraphs yet. An inner join drops it from the audit. A left join keeps that document with an empty child field. You can see one row. How many paragraphs should the audit report for this draft?
Count the child identity and the result is zero. The null field represents the missing paragraph. Counting every joined row with count star gives one because the draft itself survived the join.

title: Filter rows before counting groups

beats.say: Which Harbor sources have at least two current paragraphs on August twelfth? Two editions share the title Return Policy. Look at their IDs and dates. The older edition ended on July first. WHERE chooses input rows, so its paragraph drops out.

GROUP BY gathers the remaining paragraphs by document ID and title. Count the cards in each group. The July return policy has two. The staff guide has one. HAVING tests those counts. Only the July return policy meets the cutoff of two.

To include an empty source, begin with documents and LEFT JOIN matching children. Put a child-selection condition in that join when empty parents must remain. COUNT of the child identity ignores the NULL placeholder, so the empty source has zero children.
COUNT star counts the retained joined row and gives one. Moving the child condition into WHERE can remove that placeholder and lose the empty source entirely.

title: What still points to Acme’s policy?

beats.say: Look at Acme’s API Key Policy in the SQLite lab. Try deleting its document while two chunks still point to it. SQLite rejects the deletion. Try deleting those chunks. Four permission rows still point to them, so that fails too.

Remove the grants, then the chunks, then the document in one transaction. Roll back the rehearsal. The document, both chunks and all four grants return. Harbor’s return policy has the same dependency.

ON DELETE CASCADE can automate a declared foreign-key action, but this schema did not declare it. Choose deletion or historical retention deliberately. A database cascade also does not delete a remote vector entry, object-store copy or application cache. Coordinate those stores with explicit operations and observable completion.

Keeping an old edition also lets us answer an earlier policy-time query. Suppose Acme audits June thirtieth. Its January API policy said ninety days. Move the request to July first. That old interval ends and the seven-day rule takes over. Both documents can stay in the archive.

title: What survives a duplicate insert?

beats.say: Imagine two empty tables, each with a unique key. Put one K in each table. In the lab’s Python legacy transaction mode, that first write opens a transaction. Try to insert the same K again. Both tables reject the duplicate.
On the left the handler catches the error inside the with block. On the right the handler waits outside. When both blocks finish, where will the first K still exist?

Follow the error out to each handler. On the left the block finishes normally, so the earlier insert commits. On the right the error crosses the block boundary, and Python rolls back the open transaction. Count the saved rows. One on the left. Zero on the right.
To roll back a whole failed ingestion, let the exception reach the transaction boundary and handle it outside.
The connection’s with block handles the exit of an open transaction. The first write opened it here. Python’s autocommit setting matters, and the program still has to close the connection itself.

title: Publish one complete policy edition

beats.say: A writer is about to publish the August edition. Leave the July book open in front of the first reader. There are two paragraphs. In SQLite’s write-ahead logging mode, that read transaction can stay open while the writer commits. The writer closes the old interval and stages the replacement in one transaction. Only that writer sees the unfinished rows.

Suppose a new paragraph names a missing document. The foreign key rejects that statement. Earlier writes are still pending until we roll back the transaction. Watch the staged document disappear and the old end time return. The other reader's complete policy has stayed available.

Retry with the correct references. Assemble the deadline, receipt, and clothing paragraphs, with a grant for Bob on each. Commit the edition. Look at the first reader. Both July paragraphs are still there in its open transaction. A second reader now begins a fresh read.

The second reader sees all three August paragraphs at once. Read across the two editions. Both deadlines say fourteen days. The tags instruction appears only in August. The old paragraph IDs still trace the earlier answer.

A publisher also needs concurrency control around this version replacement. In our SQLite reference, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claims the writer slot before checking the open edition. A competing writer waits or retries. The transaction covers these local rows; remote embedding work needs its own publication workflow.

title: What can the second connection read?

beats.say: Harbor committed its new return policy. In the article’s SQLite exercise, Acme rehearses a change to its API key policy using two connections to the same file. The writer closes the old edition at the request time. Run its query before it inserts the replacement.
It gets an empty result. At that instant, what would the second connection read?

Ask the second connection. It still gets the seven-day edition. The writer can now stage the replacement, its paragraph and its reader grant. The writer sees five days. The other connection’s earlier read can still be traced to the original seven-day row.
End the rehearsal with a rollback. The old edition is active again on the writer too.

How did Acme keep two publishers from checking the same open edition at once? The first one took SQLite’s writer slot before it looked. Let a second publisher try for that slot with zero wait time. SQLite reports busy.

A real publisher can wait within a limit or retry the whole publication. On PostgreSQL a serialization failure also calls for a whole-transaction retry. If publishing starts a remote embedding job, stage that work separately or use an outbox with an idempotent consumer.

title: Can the export use its first count?

beats.say: The evaluation team wants a list of every current Harbor paragraph, including the staff guide. This is a corpus export. Start its count before the new edition commits. Keep that number on the page. While the export is waiting to fetch its list, the publisher has time to finish. Will the list fit the count?

The publisher commits the new edition. Find the line for clothing tags. It had no paragraph before. Now run the detail query. In PostgreSQL’s Read Committed mode that statement sees what was committed when it began. Four rows go beside a count of three. Both reads saw complete editions.

Replay the same publication with a read-only Repeatable Read transaction. Its first query fixed the snapshot at the count. Send the detail query back to that same picture. The IDs beside the second count are the ones that were there when it was taken.

The writer still committed. This export can finish describing the earlier edition. A third count in the same read-only Repeatable Read transaction still sees three. Under Read Committed the third count takes a fresh snapshot. No one has written since the detail query, so it counts four.

title: Can the worker reuse this request key?

beats.say: The publication committed, but its reply was lost. A worker sends the request again. Save a unique request identity and a fingerprint of every input field in the same transaction as the publication. That durable marker tells the next worker which operation already completed.

Compare the arriving input with the stored fingerprint. Identical input reuses the retained result. Watch the reply return while the document and paragraph rows stay unchanged. A transaction made the first attempt complete; the unique marker recognizes the repeat.

Now change the clothing paragraph while keeping the request identity. Its fingerprint changes. Reject that reuse and preserve the committed publication. To publish the revision, prepare a new request. Give it a fresh key and name the current edition as its predecessor.

Give the replacement a later start and a new document ID. Give each new chunk its own ID. The fingerprint compares content. The service must authenticate the caller and check permission to publish in the requested workspace.

title: What happens if the reply gets lost?

beats.say: Acme gets the same request twice. The importer fingerprints all seven fields of the policy request. It saves the key and fingerprint with the document and paragraph in one transaction. Try the same key and the same input. The importer skips the write.
Change just the paragraph text under that key. The fingerprint changes and the importer rejects the request. The original paragraph stays private. Bob needs a grant to read it.

Now send the paragraph to an embedding service. The service starts job forty-two and saves its number under the request key. Its reply gets lost. The worker’s job number is still blank. How can the worker find the job it already started?

Send the same key again. The service looks up its receipt and sends back forty-two. The worker records that number. One job serves both attempts. An outbox can keep the request ready for retry. The receiving service needs to recognize the key each time.

In this example the service retained a receipt. If the destination has no such contract and the reply goes missing, check its actual state before retrying. A blank local record leaves the outcome unknown. Before accepting a publication, the server identifies the caller and checks write permission for Acme’s workspace.

title: Change the path while keeping the answer fixed

beats.say: Go back to Harbor's seven permission rows before publication. We'll use this same copy for both searches. A table scan can inspect every permission row. Build an additional index ordered by reader and paragraph identity. Now seek the start of Bob's range.
The rows are still in the table. The index tells us where to look.

Bob's range contains four candidates. One is a retired Harbor paragraph. Another belongs to Birch. The same two paragraphs pass the workspace and time checks as before. You can read both IDs beside the text. Those counts describe candidates and results.
Reading the index takes work too, and every change to a grant has to update it.

SQLite's actual plan names the permission index it searches. A plan tells us the access strategy. Benchmark representative data to learn the latency. An ordinary reader index also leaves substring text matching as separate work. Correct results stay fixed while we test faster access.

title: What work does the database do?

beats.say: Start with Bob’s name. The first line finds him in the permission index. His entry already contains the chunk ID. That makes this a covering index for the permission lookup. Follow the chunk ID to the paragraph. Its document ID leads to the title.
The last line builds a temporary B-tree to put the results in order.

SQLite calls a full walk through a table or index a scan. A search visits a subset. Of seven grants, four name Bob. Two lead to current Harbor paragraphs. Now look for the word turn. It even matches inside the word return.
An index ordered by reader helps with Bob’s name. For frequent matches inside words, use an index designed for substrings. Each extra index takes space and work to maintain as the rows change.

Suppose we rename a policy in a PostgreSQL transaction. EXPLAIN shows the plan and estimates how many rows the update will touch. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the update and reports actual row counts and timing. The title changes to Coat Returns.

Say a function also sends an email, and it arrives. Now roll back. The old title comes back. The email stays in the inbox. To compare two plans for Bob’s search, run his SELECT with representative filters.

Check that the paragraphs match. Then compare page reads and execution times. Seven grants, four index candidates, and two results tell us how the sets narrowed. Those counts alone give no timing or page-read measurement.

title: Which neighbor can answer the customer?

beats.say: Return to the published August edition with its three Harbor return paragraphs. The customer asks, can I take this coat back? None of our paragraphs contains that phrase. An embedding model represents the question and each paragraph with a vector.

We chose these coordinates by hand so we can follow the comparison. The query points right. Look at Birch’s paragraph. Its vector goes three steps right and one up. Divide both coordinates by the square root of ten.

The tip moves onto the unit circle without changing direction. Now drop the tip onto the query axis. Its horizontal coordinate is the cosine similarity. To the left of zero, that score would be negative.
Place the other tips on the same circle and order them by that coordinate. Can Bob cite the closest paragraph for this customer?

Read the nearest row. It belongs to another store. The next is retired. The staff rule lacks Bob's grant. The request needs two results. Keep going down the ranked list. The next two current Harbor paragraphs pass all three checks.
With an approximate index you may run out of candidates before you fill both places. We can test that against an exact search.

Save the identity of the embedding that came first for Bob. Follow it to this exact paragraph, then to the Harbor edition it quotes. A later evaluation also needs the dataset, model, policy time, corpus snapshot, and settings that produced this ranking.
Change any one of those and the same question may bring back different evidence.

title: What if the query points up?

beats.say: Take the clothing-tags paragraph at the far end of that ranking. Its tip lies to the left of the old query. Keep the paragraph and its grant fixed. Turn the query upward until it’s two units high. The paragraph points mostly up, too. What will that do to its score?

Multiply corresponding coordinates and add. The horizontal pair contributes zero and the vertical pair contributes six. Divide that dot product by both lengths. The query has length two and the paragraph has length square root of ten. Its new cosine is about point nine four nine.
The distance operator in pgvector gives about point zero five one. Smaller distances come first. Subtract that distance from one and the score column gives us the similarity again.

We chose those coordinates to show the arithmetic. Cosine takes two nonzero vectors of equal dimension. To interpret the score as a match in meaning, use the model’s prescribed query and document encoders and prepare each input as the model expects.

Their outputs must share a comparable space. Store the model version, source chunk and creation time with the vector. The article declares three dimensions in PostgreSQL. We drew two. Bind the query with your driver’s placeholders and keep the workspace, time, model and reader checks.

Go back to the original query pointing right. Three paragraphs qualify for Bob. He wants the nearest two. Pgvector’s default exact search gives us that reference pair. Now try one possible HNSW scan through its graph of nearby vectors. Inspect these first three candidates.
Compare their store, edition and reader with Bob’s request. If the scan stops here, which eligible paragraphs does he get?

None of Bob’s three eligible paragraphs appears in this first group. Iterative scans let pgvector keep looking after filtering. They’re available from version zero point eight, off by default, and subject to scan limits. Continue the scan past that first group.

Both places fill, but the scan skipped the deadline paragraph. Strict distance order sorts the neighbors it found. Compare the two pairs. Only the receipt appears in both. That’s one out of two for filtered recall at two.

title: Can yesterday’s score be checked?

beats.say: Open a separate saved run with a simple pair of arrows. The query and its first hit both pointed right. Their cosine was one. A new encoder produces an arrow pointing up for that same paragraph.

What if we overwrite the stored vector so it points straight up? Follow the old result. The lookup still works, but the arrows now give zero. If the old coordinates are gone, mark the evidence as missing. The saved score tells us what the run reported. We need the original coordinates to check it. Replay that write. Keep the original row.

Give a changed encoder or preprocessing recipe its own model identifier. Store the new encoder version and its vector under a new embedding ID. The schema allows one embedding per chunk and model version.
To keep multiple revisions for that same pair, include a revision in the unique key. If the source words change, give the edited chunk a new ID too.

These two embeddings were already in the file when run one ranked the coat query. The later embedding can appear in a later run. Each result keeps its rank, score and embedding ID. The run records the dataset and query model.

Give each rank one place in this query. A second uniqueness rule keeps the same embedding from taking two places, and ranks must be positive. To repeat the search, also save the query, settings, preprocessing version, policy time and corpus snapshot.

The minimal evaluation tables in the article leave the query, settings, preprocessing version, policy time, and corpus snapshot to add. Without them a score can point to a real row while its ranking is hard to repeat.

Here’s a report for one query. In the first dataset, the deadline paragraph was marked relevant, so it earned a hit. In a second dataset the reviewer marks only the tags paragraph relevant. Look at the chunk the search returned. What score belongs beside the new labels?
This report gets zero. Bob’s first result is still the deadline paragraph. The second dataset counts only the tags paragraph as a hit. Keep both reports with the labels used to score them.

title: The coat is back on the counter

beats.say: Back to the coat bought eighteen days ago. Bob reopens the file after publication. Two paragraphs now give the same deadline. Check the edition in force at noon on August twelfth. Follow the store on that same row and look for Bob among its readers. Which paragraph belongs on the slip?
The current Harbor paragraph gives Bob fourteen days. At day eighteen, this coat is four days outside the window. The citation on the slip identifies the exact edition and paragraph Bob used.

title: A new slip on September first

beats.say: Here’s another return slip and a fresh set of policies. On August thirty-first Bob’s search returned the fourteen-day paragraph. Move the request to the first instant of September. Follow the date line through the Harbor rows, then check the reader for each paragraph. Which fields can Bob fill in now?

The old deadline ended where the new one began. Read the grant on the new deadline. It names Cara. Bob’s other deadline belongs to Birch. Run the Harbor request with Bob’s grants. He can ask for the receipt. The deadline field stays empty.

Now the policy owner authorizes Bob to retrieve the deadline too. Keep Cara’s row. Add Bob’s grant to c80. The paragraph and date stay fixed. Run the same request again. Now write ten days on the slip.
Follow the ten-day deadline back to its paragraph. Those words were already in the file. Bob can quote them now because the new grant names him.
